S&P Turns Negative on Meta. Wall Street Sees Less Than Half the Cash Hole ©Peopleimages.com - YuriArcurs and Зображення користувача Андрій Драган via Canva
Key Takeaways

S&P revised Meta's credit outlook to negative from stable on Oct. 30 and kept the AA- rating. It forecasts free operating cash flow deficits of $22 billion in 2026, $71 billion in 2027 and $39 billion in 2028.

Meta's free cash flow fell from $13.23 billion in the first quarter of 2026 to minus $1.16 billion in the third. Over the same stretch, quarterly capex reached $33.94 billion, up 80% from a year earlier.

Wall Street's estimates add up to a $61.32 billion deficit over three years, less than half of S&P's $132 billion. The biggest gap is in 2028, the year S&P's rating decision hinges on.

Meta is lining up a stock sale of up to $95 billion to fund its AI buildout. Its 2027 capex guide, due on the fourth-quarter call, will show whether S&P's forecast or the Street's is closer.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) goes into the Nov. 2 session with a credit warning attached. S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on Meta to negative from stable after the close on Oct. 30, citing uncertainty over how long heavy capital spending and negative free operating cash flow will last. It kept the AA- rating, so this is a warning, not a downgrade.

Meta closed at $614.99 that day, down 15% for October. What S&P adds is a three-year cash forecast far darker than Wall Street's.

S&P Doubts Meta Can Earn It Back Like Its Rivals

S&P's core complaint is payback. It said Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is "more limited than that of its peers," which make money leasing out compute capacity. Alphabet shows the contrast: its third-quarter free cash flow was also negative, at minus $9.1 billion, but Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion.

S&P now expects Meta to spend about $140 billion this year, more than $225 billion in 2027 and $252 billion in 2028, with free operating cash flow deficits of $22 billion, $71 billion and $39 billion. It could cut the rating if adjusted leverage stays above 1.0x and cash flow is still negative beyond 2028.

Meta pushed back. "We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," a spokesperson told Reuters. Its own CFO was more measured. On theQ3 earnings call on Oct. 21, Susan Li said Meta's AI lab investments "will take longer to generate returns than those in our core business."

Meta's Cash Cushion Was Gone Before S&P Acted

Through 2024 and 2025, Meta's free cash flow ran between $9.02 billion and $16.47 billion a quarter on TIKR's measure. Then it fell off a ledge: $13.23 billion in the first quarter of 2026, $1.75 billion in the second and minus $1.16 billion in the third. (Meta's own count, which also subtracts finance lease payments, was minus $2.12 billion.)

title: Here's Where I Think Meta Stock Will Be in 2030

Here's Where I Think Meta Stock Will Be in 2030
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 2:57 AM CST 5 min read
META
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares in Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) cost about $612 as I write. The stock has dropped around 22% from its August 2025 record close of $790, even as third-quarter revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion.

Much of the gap probably boils down to spending and new shares. Meta expects 2026 capital expenditures (counting finance-lease principal payments) of $135 billion to $145 billion. And on Oct. 26, it priced a $25 billion stock sale at $625 a share, with plans to sell up to about $60 billion more later.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Using an earnings path based on the company's own trend and guidance, I think Meta stock could trade near $880 in late 2030. That would be about 44% above today's price, or a bit over 9% a year -- a solid return, but arguably less than Meta's sales growth alone might suggest.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Revenue may reach about $435 billion

The social media company's revenue growth is slowing, though just a bit at a time. It was 33% year over year in the first quarter of 2026 before cooling to 28% and then 26%. And its guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion for the fourth quarter points to around 22% to 27%.

Add the guidance to the $181.7 billion in sales Meta posted through September, and 2026 revenue totals around $255 billion to $258 billion, up about 27% to 28% over 2025.

Management said in the third-quarter earnings release that it expects to "sustain strong overall revenue growth throughout 2027." I assumed growth keeps cooling from there: 20% in 2027, 15% in 2028, 12% in 2029, and 10% in 2030. And this takes revenue to around $435 billion in 2030, about 70% over this year's level.

Margins are the tougher call

Meta's spending is now showing up in its expenses. Depreciation on its property and equipment jumped 43% year over year to $6.81 billion in the third quarter. Leaving out the $9.89 billion charge Meta took for its August deal with state attorneys general (a cost I'm counting as one-off), the operating margin was about 35%. It was down from 40% a year before and 41% for all of 2025.

True, Meta expects Reality Labs losses to fall to roughly $15 billion in 2027, from $18 billion to $19 billion in 2026. But it also plans to keep "investing aggressively" next year.

I used a 35% operating margin for 2030, or about $152 billion of operating income. After a tax rate of about 16% (in line with Meta's fourth-quarter forecast) and a few billion dollars of interest and other costs, net income is near $125 billion.

Josh Brown: Meta Could Become "a Cash Spigot" That Makes Nvidia Look Expensive ©Diego Maravilla from Diego Maravilla via Canva
Key Takeaways

On Prof G Markets, Josh Brown said Anthropic could become "a cash spigot" priced to make Nvidia and Palantir look expensive. He listed Meta's push into AI agents as one of its threats.

Brown also named Meta and Alphabet as his two public examples of a company with a premier AI model and its own compute, which makes Meta a better fit for his case than the AI lab he was describing.

Analysts expect Meta's normalized EPS to rise from $29.68 in 2025 to $42.30 in 2028, and the stock trades at 19x forward earnings, below its five-year average of 21x.

The catch is cash: analysts don't expect Meta's free cash flow to recover until 2029, and the 2027 capex plan due in late January is the next test.

Josh Brown sees "a cash spigot" coming in AI. He was talking about Anthropic, but the company that fits his description best is Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ).

On the Oct. 30 episode of Prof G Markets, Brown, who co-hosts The Compound and Friends, walked through Anthropic's IPO filing. He said Anthropic is priced below Palantir and about in line with Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ), while growing much faster than both. (Nvidia, for its part, agreed last week to put $3 billion into Meta's stock sale.)

Then he listed what could go wrong. One threat on his list: "if Facebook takes advantage of the agentic layer and connects the 500 million businesses they already have a relationship with, with the 3 billion consumers."

If Anthropic gets past all of that, he said, "this thing becomes a cash spigot trading at a multiple that makes Nvidia" look expensive, "and especially Palantir."

So why not just own the threat?

Brown got there himself later in the episode: "I have two examples in the publicly traded market of a company that has a premier model and its own source of compute to run that model. We have obviously Alphabet and Google Gemini and now we have Meta and Muse."

Anthropic, he pointed out, has to pay someone else for its compute. Meta builds most of its own, though not all: Susan Li said higher third-party cloud spend helped drive its third-quarter cost growth.

Brown's Numbers Hold Up

Based on a user survey, Meta estimates that at least 500 million self-identified small businesses use its apps, a figure it repeated in its Oct. 26 offering document. Those apps averaged 3.64 billion daily users in September.

Muse, its new agent, is already putting the two together. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada set it up in its first six weeks. Management said on the third-quarter call that over a quarter of active users shop with it, spending more than $200 per purchase on average (travel bookings included).

title: After Meta, Could These Be Wall Street’s Next Blockbuster Stock Splits?
detail:
After Meta, Could These Be Wall Street’s Next Blockbuster Stock Splits?
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 3:53 PM CDT 5 min read
META
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Could stock-split mania take over Wall Street in the next few years? On the one hand, many corporations are capitalizing on artificial intelligence (AI) and have seen their share prices soar, potentially triggering a wave of blockbuster stock splits. And one could also argue that Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) just kicked things off by announcing a 2-for-1 stock split that will create a brand-new category of non-voting shares.

That will allow the tech leader to issue shares to finance its AI-related ambitions without reducing the voting power of its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

However, it is always hard to predict upcoming stock splits, even if some signs point in that direction. That said, if there are more stock splits on the horizon, here are two companies that could join the club: Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) and MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI).

Image source: The Motley Fool.

1. Micron Technology

Micron Technology designs and sells computer memory chips. Demand for the company's products has soared amid the massive ongoing AI build-out, and the semiconductor specialist is reaping the benefits. Micron's revenue and net income have reached all-time highs.

MU Revenue (Annual) data by YCharts

What's more, the AI tailwind could be far from over. Not only are Micron's chips in high demand, but there is also a severe shortage, giving it significant pricing power. Consider, for instance, that Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) increased its capex guidance for 2026 from $200 billion to $220 billion, partly due to higher memory chip prices. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), another hyperscaler, also attributed some of its massive capex guidance for the year to rising memory chip prices. This helps highlight the scale of the opportunity for Micron.

Further, the shortage of memory chips might last at least a couple more years. Micron's shares have gained significant value this year on the back of excellent financial results, and despite a pullback in recent months, the company's prospects remain bright.

Shares are currently changing hands for about $983 apiece. Of course, there is no generally agreed-upon price at which a company must split its stock. Still, if Micron performs well over the next year or two and continues to capitalize on the soaring demand for its products, the company could decide to split its stock.

Meta's results a week earlier had revived worries about Big Tech's AI spending.

Alphabet's Search Slowed as Spending Soared

Search & other grew 12% to $63.4 billion, about $1.5 billion short of estimates and down from 17% in the second quarter.

That came even as CEO Sundar Pichai said query growth was "the highest it's been in the last five years." Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler blamed currency, plus lower monetization in AI Mode. The second reason worries me: Google is answering more questions than ever but earning less on each AI answer than on a classic search.

Capex hit $51.4 billion, above the $42.3 billion of cash from operations, so free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion, its second negative quarter in a row.

Meta showed the same squeeze on Oct. 21: its $34.9 billion of third-quarter capex topped its $32.8 billion of operating cash flow, and it narrowed its 2026 capex range to $135 billion to $145 billion. Meta stock is down 15% over the month. How long can each ad business carry the build?

And CFO Anat Ashkenazi expects Alphabet's capex "to increase significantly in 2027." TIKR's consensus has normalized EPS at $15.14 a share in 2027 and $18.26 in 2028:

GOOG Normalized EPS Estimates: 2024-2029 (TIKR)
Cramer's Half Right

Cloud revenue grew 103% to $30.7 billion, and its operating margin rose to 36.2% from 23.7%. But "lost" goes too far: Google Services still earned $39.2 billion of operating income, more than three times Cloud's $11.1 billion.
